trial_name: SOAP II — Comparison of Dopamine and Norepinephrine in the Treatment of Shock (2010)
citation: De Backer D, Biston P, Devriendt J, et al. Comparison of dopamine and norepinephrine in the treatment of shock. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(9):779-789.
one_liner: In ICU shock, dopamine did not improve 28-day mortality vs. norepinephrine but caused more arrhythmias, making norepinephrine the safer first-line vasopressor.

pico.population: Adults in ICU with shock (MAP <70 mmHg or SBP <100 mmHg after fluids, plus hypoperfusion signs)
pico.intervention: Dopamine infusion (weight-based, max 20 mcg/kg/min) with open‑label norepinephrine rescue
pico.comparison: Norepinephrine infusion (weight-based, max 0.19 mcg/kg/min) with open‑label norepinephrine rescue
pico.outcome: 28‑day all‑cause mortality (primary); arrhythmias, ICU/hospital/6‑month/12‑month mortality, days without vasopressors

background.existing_knowledge: Dopamine and norepinephrine were both widely used as first‑line vasopressors for shock, but with different pharmacology; observational data suggested potential harm with dopamine.
background.knowledge_gap: Prior comparative randomised evidence was limited, and equipoise remained over whether dopamine reduced mortality without excess adverse events.
background.hypothesis: Dopamine would reduce 28‑day mortality compared with norepinephrine in ICU shock patients without excess adverse events.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double‑blind trial with prespecified sequential (triangular‑test) monitoring design; enrolment Dec 2003 to Oct 2007.

inclusion: Shock defined as MAP <70 mmHg or SBP <100 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation (≥1000 mL crystalloids or ≥500 mL colloids, or CVP >12 mmHg/PAOP >14 mmHg)
Signs of tissue hypoperfusion: altered mental state, mottled skin, urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 1 h, or lactate >2 mmol/L
exclusion: Vasopressor therapy for >4 h in current shock episode
Serious arrhythmia (rapid atrial fibrillation >160/min, ventricular tachycardia)

methods.intervention: Dopamine infusion (weight‑based), increased by 2 mcg/kg/min up to 20 mcg/kg/min; open‑label norepinephrine permitted if target BP not reached; rescue vasopressors (epinephrine, vasopressin) and inotropes allowed.
methods.comparison: Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) infusion (weight‑based), increased by 0.02 mcg/kg/min up to 0.19 mcg/kg/min; same open‑label norepinephrine and rescue rules as dopamine arm (open‑label dopamine not permitted).
methods.blinding: Double‑blind: allocation by sealed opaque envelopes; study drug prepared by unblinded person not involved in care; clinicians, investigators, personnel remained blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: 765 per group planned to detect 15% relative reduction in 28‑day mortality (43% vs 36%) with 80% power at two‑sided α=0.05; stopped after 1679 randomised when sequential boundary indicated ‘no difference’.
secondary_outcomes: Days without need for open‑label vasopressors
Days without need for trial drug
Study‑drug discontinuation due to severe arrhythmia
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint at 28 days; secondary mortality follow‑up at ICU discharge, hospital discharge, 6 and 12 months (6‑month data available for 1443/1679, 12‑month for 1036/1679).

headline_bullets: No significant difference in 28‑day mortality: 52.5% dopamine vs 48.5% norepinephrine (OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.97–1.42, p=0.10).
Arrhythmias were more frequent with dopamine: 24.1% vs 12.4% (p<0.001), predominantly atrial fibrillation (20.5% vs 11.0%).
More study‑drug discontinuation due to severe arrhythmia with dopamine (6.1% vs 1.6%, p<0.001), increasing rescue‑therapy crossover.
A cardiogenic shock subgroup signal (log‑rank p=0.03) was not supported by a significant interaction test (p=0.87).

outcomes_table.outcome: Study drug discontinued due to severe arrhythmia
Days without need for open‑label vasopressors (mean ± SD)
outcomes_table.note: Consistent with more rescue therapy in dopamine group

outcomes_table.outcome: Days without need for trial drug (mean ± SD)

subgroup_table.note: Log‑rank P=0.03 for higher mortality with dopamine; interaction test NS.

safety: Atrial fibrillation: 20.5% of dopamine vs 11.0% of norepinephrine (driving overall arrhythmia difference).
Study‑drug discontinuation due to severe arrhythmia: 6.1% vs 1.6% (P<0.001).
No other major adverse events reported beyond the rhythm toxicity.

domains.notes: Computer‑generated sequence, permuted blocks, stratified by ICU; sealed opaque envelopes; drug prepared by unblinded person – low risk.
Double‑blind maintained; mortality objective. Clinician‑defined BP targets introduced pragmatic variability but did not affect primary outcome ascertainment.
28‑day mortality complete for all 1679 patients. 6‑ and 12‑month mortality incomplete (1443/1679 and 1036/1679 available) – some attrition risk for later endpoints.

Open‑label norepinephrine rescue more common in dopamine arm (26% vs 20%, P<0.001); severe arrhythmia led to more discontinuation in dopamine arm (52 vs 13 patients). Both attenuated treatment separation.

Groups well matched: median APACHE II 20 vs 20, SOFA 9 vs 9; shock aetiology distribution similar (septic 63.2% vs 61.1%). Some pretreatment differences: open‑label norepinephrine before enrolment 18.3% vs 13.0%, dobutamine 14.8% vs 19.4%.

internal_validity.verdict: Strong for primary mortality given blinded design, objective endpoint, and complete 28‑day follow‑up; diluted by rescue therapy and early stopping per sequential design.

domains.notes: Broad ICU shock population (septic 63.2% vs 61.1%, cardiogenic 15.7% vs 17.7%, hypovolaemic 14.7% vs 14.4%, other 6.4% vs 6.8%) with few exclusions (serious arrhythmias, prolonged prior vasopressors). Real‑world relevance high.

Conducted in European ICUs 2003–2007; co‑interventions (e.g., activated protein C in a minority) have changed, but catecholamine physiology and arrhythmia risk remain directly applicable. Generalises best to ICU shock requiring catecholamines with clinician‑titrated BP targets.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate‑to‑strong for ICU shock care: broad, pragmatic inclusion, though evolving sepsis bundles and the European ICU era slightly constrain direct transportability to all modern settings.

strengths: Prespecified sequential monitoring with predefined stopping rules
Detailed adverse‑event capture (arrhythmias) with clear between‑group separation
limitations: Pragmatic clinician‑driven BP targets and permitted rescue norepinephrine reduced contrast between strategies
Heterogeneity of shock types limits disease‑specific treatment effect estimates
Cardiogenic shock subgroup signal not supported by interaction test
Dose‑range equipotency between maximally‑dosed dopamine and norepinephrine uncertain

critical_appraisal.summary: A well‑designed, blinded RCT with complete primary outcome follow‑up that demonstrates no mortality benefit for dopamine over norepinephrine but a clear and clinically relevant excess of arrhythmias, supporting norepinephrine as the safer first‑line vasopressor.
strengths: Large sample and prespecified sequential monitoring
Detailed, unbiased capture of arrhythmic harms
weaknesses: Potential for residual confounding in cardiogenic shock subgroup

sections.authors_conclusion: Dopamine did not reduce 28‑day mortality compared with norepinephrine and was associated with significantly higher rates of arrhythmias, supporting norepinephrine as the preferred first‑line vasopressor in ICU shock.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not change the primary mortality strategy but confirms that norepinephrine is safer than dopamine as the default first‑line vasopressor in ICU shock, driven by arrhythmia risk.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU patients with shock requiring vasopressors, especially those at risk for tachyarrhythmias; limited application if dopamine is needed for chronotropy or norepinephrine is unavailable.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That dopamine is ineffective or harmful in all shock subgroups; the mortality difference was not statistically significant, and the cardiogenic shock signal is hypothesis‑generating only.
implementation_caveats: Use norepinephrine as first‑line; reserve dopamine for selected patients with low arrhythmia risk and a need for chronotropy, or when norepinephrine is unavailable.
Monitor closely for atrial fibrillation and consider rhythm‑control strategy if dopamine must be used.

controversies.topic: Pre‑randomisation catecholamine use and fluid resuscitation
controversies.notes: Editorial critique highlighted that many patients had already received open‑label vasopressors and that adequacy of fluid resuscitation could be questioned, potentially affecting generalisability.
More frequent open‑label norepinephrine use in dopamine arm (26% vs 20%) may blur comparison; sensitivity analysis excluding those patients still showed no mortality difference (P=0.45).
Higher mortality with dopamine (P=0.03) but non‑significant interaction (P=0.87) and possible unmeasured confounding (mechanical support, revascularisation details) limit causal inference.
Subsequent meta‑analysis of RCTs in septic shock reported higher mortality and substantially increased arrhythmias with dopamine vs. norepinephrine, consistent with SOAP II safety findings.
Modern sepsis guidelines recommend norepinephrine first‑line, largely based on SOAP II; cardiogenic shock guidelines similarly prefer norepinephrine over dopamine.

unresolved_questions: Is dopamine truly harmful in cardiogenic shock or merely a marker of unmeasured severity?
What is the optimal vasopressor titration strategy to minimize arrhythmias while maintaining perfusion?
How do newer vasopressors (vasopressin, angiotensin II) compare in arrhythmia risk in similar populations?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Norepinephrine is preferred over dopamine for ICU shock: similar survival but much less arrhythmia.
